title: Ashvamedhika
hook: the war is won, the funeral rites are done, and the new king falls down on the riverbank and can't get up
carry: a man who can't stand up

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma asked Krishna's leave and let go. Your line was the arrows fall from him one by one.

The water offerings for Bhishma have been poured into the Ganga. The great teacher is gone. Yudhishthira has listened to him at length, about kingship, duty and peace. He has the crown and the kingdom. And at the riverbank, in Ganguli's telling, he simply goes down, collapsing on the bank, overwhelmed by grief. Bhima holds him. Krishna speaks to him. And the old blind king Dhritarashtra, whose own sons died in this war, is the one who tells him to get up. A new book opens with a king on the ground.
screen: `THE OFFERINGS ARE POURED.` → `THE KING FALLS ON THE BANK.` → `THE BLIND KING SAYS: GET UP.`

segments.voice: Ashvamedhika is the book of the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice: a great royal rite in which a consecrated horse wanders free, guarded by warriors, and the kingdoms it passes through either welcome it or fight. The idea isn't Yudhishthira's. He wants to leave the throne for the forest. It's the sage Vyasa who tells him that grief is not a plan. Perform sacrifices, Vyasa says, give gifts, take up a king's work; the horse sacrifice will cleanse what weighs on you. Yudhishthira's answer is practical. There's no money. The war has emptied the treasury, the kings who might have sent tribute are dead, and he will not squeeze grieving people for more. So Vyasa tells an old story. Long ago, King Marutta held a sacrifice in the Himalayas so lavish that the gold left behind was too much to carry away. It's still there in the mountains, Vyasa says. Go and bring it. The victors don't get a parade. They get a man who can't stand up, an empty treasury, and a sage pointing at an old king's leftover gold. The way forward runs through someone else's generosity, long ago. In the days ahead, this book brings a forgotten teaching, an angry sage, a child who comes back to life, a son who fights his father, and a strange little animal with half a golden body. It begins with getting up.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHA: THE HORSE SACRIFICE` · `VYASA: GRIEF IS NOT A PLAN` · `"THE TREASURY IS EMPTY"` · then, large: `MARUTTA'S GOLD IN THE MOUNTAINS`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind a time you knew what to do next and simply couldn't stand up to do it, and who helped you to your feet, or who you wish had. Breathe out, let your shoulders drop, and hold the name of one person near you who may be on the riverbank right now; if you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Ashvamedhika. The book of the horse sacrifice, which begins with a grieving king and an empty treasury.
Your line: a man who can't stand up. The book of the horse begins on the ground. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Ashvamedhika Parva is the book of the Mahabharata that follows Bhishma's teachings; Hindus hear it in recitations of the full epic, and the horse sacrifice is remembered as a great royal rite of the Vedic world.

what it means: it opens with a king who can't get up and a treasury with nothing in it.

chat.says: After winning the war, why did Yudhishthira need a horse sacrifice at all?
options: Grief had flattened him, and Vyasa urged the rite to cleanse what weighed on him.
The treasury was overflowing, and he wanted a grand way to spend it.
Bhishma ordered it with his last words before he died.
chat.meaning: At the opening of the Ashvamedhika, Yudhishthira collapses in grief, and Vyasa urges the horse sacrifice to cleanse what weighs on him.

Ashvamedhika.meaning: the epic's book of the horse sacrifice

Marutta.meaning: an ancient king whose great sacrifice left gold in the Himalayas

Vyasa.meaning: the sage credited with the Mahabharata, who also appears in its story

recall: the divine coming down in a form

notes: All paraphrase of Ganguli. Confirm the order of speakers at the opening (Yudhishthira falls on the Ganga's bank, Bhima holds him, Krishna and Dhritarashtra console him).

Confirm Vyasa's framing that the sacrifice cleanses Yudhishthira of the burden of the war, and that Marutta's gold lies in the Himalayas.
